content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /tmp/claude-1000/bundled-skills/2.1.330/1559d99a04a43cc308fb685244490b2b/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
   One exception to direct name labels: the tall segmented bar (*Figures* in `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`).
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
  One exception, legend kept: the tall segmented bar (*Figures* in `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`).
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical, except that dark-mode good is the series green |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

"""Summarise the benchmark samples, classify their distributions and draw the charts.

Usage (from the repo root, after the three benchmark runs; see bench/README.md):

    uv run --python 3.12 --with numpy --with scipy --with matplotlib \
        python -I bench/analyze.py

Reads   bench/results/{pymusic,numpy,musicrs}.csv  (one row per timed call)
Writes  bench/results/summary.csv            (every statistic, machine-readable)
        bench/results/summary.md             (the tables in the README)
        docs/benchmark{,-dark}.svg           (mean and p5 – p95 per case, log time axis)
        docs/benchmark-distribution{,-dark}.svg  (histograms of t / median)

Scheduling noise (preemption, interrupts, frequency changes) only ever adds time, so it shows
up as a right tail: mean > median, positive skew and a few slow outliers. Besides mean,
stddev and median, the summary therefore reports
  * the spread around the median (MAD, p5/p95, min/max),
  * the shape (skewness, excess kurtosis, Shapiro-Wilk tests on t and on log t, and whether
    a normal or a log-normal fit has the lower AIC),
  * outliers: calls slower than median + 3 * 1.4826 * MAD (3 robust sigmas), their share,
    and how much they raise the mean ("tail excess": mean of all calls over the mean of the
    calls that are not outliers),
  * run order: lag-1 autocorrelation and drift (mean of the last 10 % of calls over the
    first 10 %). Scheduling noise hits calls independently; a regime change (CPU frequency,
    thermal state, migration to another core) makes neighbouring calls alike instead.
"""

import csv
import math
import os
from collections import defaultdict

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("svg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # noqa: E402
import numpy as np  # noqa: E402
from scipy import stats  # noqa: E402

RESULTS = "bench/results"
DOCS = "docs"
# Display order. "numpy" is pyMUSIC's algorithm vectorized (bench/bench_numpy.py): the baseline
# that separates what Rust buys from what pyMUSIC's per-angle Python loop costs.
IMPLS = ["pymusic", "numpy", "musicrs"]
LABEL = {"pymusic": "pyMUSIC", "numpy": "numpy (vectorized)", "musicrs": "musicrs"}
BASELINES = ["pymusic", "numpy"]
WORKLOADS = [
    ("narrowband", "Narrowband DOA"),
    ("ifb_one_bin", "IFB-MUSIC, 1 bin"),
    ("ifb_all_bins", "IFB-MUSIC, 80 bins"),
]

# Reference palette of the dataviz method: categorical slots 1-3, chart chrome and ink. The light
# aqua is below 3:1 against the surface, so every mark carries a direct value label.
THEMES = {
    "light": dict(surface="#fcfcfb", ink="#0b0b0b", ink2="#52514e", muted="#898781",
                  grid="#e1e0d9", axis="#c3c2b7", musicrs="#2a78d6", pymusic="#eb6834",
                  numpy="#1baf7a"),
    "dark": dict(surface="#1a1a19", ink="#f0efec", ink2="#c3c2b7", muted="#898781",
                 grid="#2c2c2a", axis="#383835", musicrs="#3987e5", pymusic="#d95926",
                  numpy="#199e70"),
}


def load():
    samples = defaultdict(list)
    for impl in IMPLS:
        with open(os.path.join(RESULTS, f"{impl}.csv")) as f:
            for row in csv.DictReader(f):
                samples[(impl, row["workload"], row["recording_s"])].append(float(row["seconds"]))
    return {k: np.array(v) for k, v in samples.items()}


def describe(t):
    med = float(np.median(t))
    mad = float(np.median(np.abs(t - med))) * 1.4826  # scaled to sigma for normal data
    outliers = t > med + 3 * mad if mad > 0 else np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    mean = float(t.mean())
    # Shapiro-Wilk is only defined for 3..5000 samples
    sw = t[:5000]
    p_norm = float(stats.shapiro(sw).pvalue)
    p_lognorm = float(stats.shapiro(np.log(sw)).pvalue)
    # AIC of maximum-likelihood fits (2 parameters each; log-normal with loc fixed at 0)
    mu, sd = stats.norm.fit(t)
    aic_norm = 4 - 2 * stats.norm.logpdf(t, mu, sd).sum()
    shape, _, scale = stats.lognorm.fit(t, floc=0)
    aic_lognorm = 4 - 2 * stats.lognorm.logpdf(t, shape, 0, scale).sum()
    return dict(
        n=len(t),
        mean=mean,
        std=float(t.std(ddof=1)),
        cv=float(t.std(ddof=1)) / mean,
        median=med,
        mad=mad,
        min=float(t.min()),
        p5=float(np.percentile(t, 5)),
        p95=float(np.percentile(t, 95)),
        max=float(t.max()),
        skew=float(stats.skew(t)),
        kurtosis=float(stats.kurtosis(t)),
        shapiro_p_normal=p_norm,
        shapiro_p_lognormal=p_lognorm,
        better_fit="log-normal" if aic_lognorm < aic_norm else "normal",
        outlier_share=float(outliers.mean()),
        tail_excess=mean / float(t[~outliers].mean()) - 1,
        # In run order: independent noise has ~0 autocorrelation and no drift; a step or trend
        # (CPU frequency, thermal state, a move to another core) shows up in both
        autocorr_lag1=float(np.corrcoef(t[:-1], t[1:])[0, 1]),
        drift=float(t[-max(1, len(t) // 10):].mean() / t[: max(1, len(t) // 10)].mean()) - 1,
    )


def shape_verdict(s):
    """One phrase for the README table."""
    if s["shapiro_p_normal"] > 0.05:
        return "consistent with normal"
    if s["shapiro_p_lognormal"] > 0.05:
        return "consistent with log-normal"
    tail = "right-skewed" if s["skew"] > 0.5 else "skewed left" if s["skew"] < -0.5 else "near-symmetric"
    heavy = ", heavy tail" if s["kurtosis"] > 3 else ""
    return f"{tail}{heavy}, not normal (closer to {s['better_fit']})"


def fmt_time(x):
    if x >= 1:
        return f"{x:.2f} s"
    if x >= 1e-3:
        return f"{x * 1e3:.3g} ms" if x * 1e3 < 100 else f"{x * 1e3:.0f} ms"
    return f"{x * 1e6:.0f} µs"


def fmt_speedup(ratio):
    """musicrs's speedup over a baseline; below 1 means musicrs is slower."""
    return f"{ratio:,.0f}×" if ratio >= 10 else f"{ratio:.2f}×"


def relation(ratio, baseline):
    """'28× faster than pyMUSIC' / '1.4× slower than numpy', for musicrs."""
    if ratio >= 1:
        return f"{fmt_speedup(ratio)} faster than {baseline}"
    return f"{fmt_speedup(1 / ratio)} slower than {baseline}"


def cases(samples):
    """(workload key, label, recording) in display order, for the cases every implementation ran."""
    out = []
    for key, label in WORKLOADS:
        for rec in sorted({r for (_, w, r) in samples if w == key}):
            if all((impl, key, rec) in samples for impl in IMPLS):
                out.append((key, f"{label} · {float(rec):g} s recording", rec))
    return out


def style(ax, th):
    ax.set_facecolor(th["surface"])
    for side in ("top", "right", "left"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(th["axis"])
    ax.tick_params(colors=th["muted"], length=0, labelsize=9)


def time_chart(samples, summary, theme, path):
    th = THEMES[theme]
    rows = cases(samples)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.6, 1.15 * len(rows) + 1.3), dpi=100)
    fig.patch.set_facecolor(th["surface"])
    style(ax, th)
    ax.grid(axis="x", which="major", color=th["grid"], linewidth=1)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)

    # Log time axis: the three implementations span four decades (pyMUSIC's 11.5 s next to
    # sub-millisecond calls), and on a log axis equal ratios are equal distances. Dots, not
    # bars, because a bar's length means nothing on a log axis.
    offsets = {"pymusic": 0.28, "numpy": 0.0, "musicrs": -0.28}
    for i, (key, label, rec) in enumerate(rows):
        y0 = len(rows) - 1 - i
        for impl in IMPLS:
            s = summary[(impl, key, rec)]
            y = y0 + offsets[impl]
            ax.plot([s["p5"], s["p95"]], [y, y], color=th[impl], linewidth=2,
                    solid_capstyle="round", zorder=2)
            ax.plot(s["mean"], y, "o", color=th[impl], markersize=7,
                    markeredgecolor=th["surface"], markeredgewidth=1.5, zorder=3)
            ax.text(s["p95"] * 1.12, y, fmt_time(s["mean"]), va="center", ha="left",
                    fontsize=8.5, color=th["ink2"])
        musicrs = summary[("musicrs", key, rec)]["mean"]
        notes = [relation(summary[(b, key, rec)]["mean"] / musicrs, LABEL[b].split(" ")[0])
                 for b in BASELINES]
        ax.text(1.02, y0 + 0.14, notes[1], transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), va="center",
                ha="left", fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold", color=th["ink"])
        ax.text(1.02, y0 - 0.16, notes[0], transform=ax.get_yaxis_transform(), va="center",
                ha="left", fontsize=8.5, color=th["ink2"])

    ax.set_yticks(range(len(rows)))
    ax.set_yticklabels([r[1] for r in reversed(rows)], fontsize=9.5, color=th["ink"])
    ax.set_ylim(-0.6, len(rows) - 0.4)
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_xlim(2e-4, 60)
    ticks = [1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1, 1, 10]
    ax.set_xticks(ticks)
    ax.set_xticklabels(["1 ms", "10 ms", "100 ms", "1 s", "10 s"])
    ax.xaxis.set_minor_locator(matplotlib.ticker.NullLocator())
    ax.set_xlabel("Time per call, log scale (dot: mean, line: p5 – p95)",
                  color=th["muted"], fontsize=9)
    handles = [matplotlib.lines.Line2D([], [], marker="o", linestyle="", markersize=7,
                                       color=th[impl], label=LABEL[impl]) for impl in IMPLS]
    leg = ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0, 1.0), ncol=3,
                    frameon=False, fontsize=9.5, handletextpad=0.3)
    for t in leg.get_texts():
        t.set_color(th["ink"])
    fig.suptitle("Runtime per call: musicrs vs pyMUSIC and vectorized numpy", x=0.01, ha="left",
                 fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=th["ink"])
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(path, facecolor=th["surface"], metadata={"Date": None})
    plt.close(fig)


def distribution_chart(samples, summary, theme, path):
    th = THEMES[theme]
    rows = cases(samples)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(rows), len(IMPLS), figsize=(10.2, 1.45 * len(rows) + 0.9), dpi=100,
                             sharex=True)
    fig.patch.set_facecolor(th["surface"])
    edges = np.linspace(0.8, 2.0, 61)  # t / median, overflow folded into the last bin
    for i, (key, label, rec) in enumerate(rows):
        for j, impl in enumerate(IMPLS):
            ax = axes[i, j]
            style(ax, th)
            ax.set_yticks([])
            t = samples[(impl, key, rec)]
            s = summary[(impl, key, rec)]
            rel = np.clip(t / s["median"], edges[0], edges[-1] - 1e-9)
            ax.hist(rel, bins=edges, color=th[impl], linewidth=0, rwidth=0.85)
            ax.axvline(1.0, color=th["ink2"], linewidth=1)
            ax.axvline(s["mean"] / s["median"], color=th["ink"], linewidth=1, linestyle=(0, (1, 1.5)))
            ax.text(0.99, 0.92,
                    f"n = {s['n']}  ·  CV {s['cv']:.1%}\nskew {s['skew']:.1f}  ·  outliers {s['outlier_share']:.1%}",
                    transform=ax.transAxes, ha="right", va="top", fontsize=7.5, color=th["ink2"])
            if j == 0:
                ax.set_title(label, loc="left", fontsize=9, color=th["ink"], pad=3)
            if i == 0:
                ax.text(0, 1.32, LABEL[impl], transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=10.5,
                        fontweight="bold", color=th["ink"])
    for ax in axes[-1]:
        ax.set_xticks([0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.4, 1.6, 1.8, 2.0])
        ax.set_xticklabels(["0.8", "1 = median", "1.2", "1.4", "1.6", "1.8", "≥ 2"])
        ax.set_xlabel("time / median  (solid line: median, dotted: mean)", color=th["muted"], fontsize=8.5)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.2)
    fig.savefig(path, facecolor=th["surface"], metadata={"Date": None})
    plt.close(fig)


def write_tables(samples, summary):
    keys = list(next(iter(summary.values())).keys())
    with open(os.path.join(RESULTS, "summary.csv"), "w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["implementation", "workload", "recording_s", *keys])
        for (impl, key, rec), s in sorted(summary.items()):
            w.writerow([impl, key, rec, *[s[k] for k in keys]])

    # Speedup of musicrs over the row's implementation (mean time); below 1× musicrs is slower
    lines = ["| Workload | Implementation | n | Mean ± stddev | Median | p5 – p95 | CV | musicrs speedup (mean) |",
             "|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|"]
    for key, label, rec in cases(samples):
        musicrs = summary[("musicrs", key, rec)]["mean"]
        for impl in IMPLS:
            s = summary[(impl, key, rec)]
            speedup = fmt_speedup(s["mean"] / musicrs) if impl in BASELINES else ""
            lines.append(
                f"| {label if impl == IMPLS[0] else ''} | {LABEL[impl]} | {s['n']} | "
                f"{fmt_time(s['mean'])} ± {fmt_time(s['std'])} | {fmt_time(s['median'])} | "
                f"{fmt_time(s['p5'])} – {fmt_time(s['p95'])} | {s['cv']:.1%} | {speedup} |")
    lines += ["", "| Workload | Implementation | Shape | Skew | Excess kurtosis | Shapiro p (t / log t) | (Mean − median) / median | Outliers | Tail excess | Lag-1 autocorr. | Drift |",
              "|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|"]
    for key, label, rec in cases(samples):
        for impl in IMPLS:
            s = summary[(impl, key, rec)]
            lines.append(
                f"| {label if impl == IMPLS[0] else ''} | {LABEL[impl]} | {shape_verdict(s)} | "
                f"{s['skew']:.2f} | {s['kurtosis']:.1f} | "
                f"{s['shapiro_p_normal']:.2g} / {s['shapiro_p_lognormal']:.2g} | "
                f"{(s['mean'] - s['median']) / s['median']:+.1%} | {s['outlier_share']:.1%} | "
                f"{s['tail_excess']:+.1%} | {s['autocorr_lag1']:.2f} | {s['drift']:+.1%} |")
    with open(os.path.join(RESULTS, "summary.md"), "w") as f:
        f.write("\n".join(lines) + "\n")
    print("\n".join(lines))


def main():
    plt.rcParams.update({"svg.fonttype": "none", "svg.hashsalt": "musicrs-bench",
                         "font.family": "sans-serif"})
    samples = load()
    summary = {k: describe(v) for k, v in samples.items()}
    write_tables(samples, summary)
    os.makedirs(DOCS, exist_ok=True)
    for theme in THEMES:
        suffix = "" if theme == "light" else "-dark"
        time_chart(samples, summary, theme, os.path.join(DOCS, f"benchmark{suffix}.svg"))
        distribution_chart(samples, summary, theme,
                           os.path.join(DOCS, f"benchmark-distribution{suffix}.svg"))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

55:## Performance vs pyMUSIC
- IFB-MUSIC only sees frequencies up to Nyquist (`sample_rate / 2`); a tone recorded above
  Nyquist is aliased and its DOA cannot be recovered from the STFT bins.
- Running IFB-MUSIC over *all* bins on a narrowband signal is dominated by noise-only bins;
  select the bins that carry signal energy.

## Performance vs pyMUSIC

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="docs/benchmark-dark.svg">
  <img alt="Bar chart of time per call on a linear scale; every bar except pyMUSIC's IFB-MUSIC over 80 bins is only a few pixels wide or less, and value labels give the numbers. musicrs is 28× faster than pyMUSIC for narrowband DOA on a 1 s recording, 14× on a 2 s recording, 191× and 122× for single-bin IFB-MUSIC, and 784× for IFB-MUSIC over 80 bins (11.5 s vs 14.7 ms)." src="docs/benchmark.svg">
</picture>

The same calls on the same recordings (1400 Hz, 40°), from the real-valued samples to the
result, with pyMUSIC run unmodified. musicrs is **14× to 784× faster** by mean time per call.
pyMUSIC spends ~140 ms per pseudo-spectrum building 720 `float128` steering vectors in a
Python loop, whatever the recording length, so the gap is widest for IFB-MUSIC (one spectrum
per bin) and narrows for longer recordings, where musicrs's own work (Hilbert transform,
covariance) grows with the sample count.

Schmidt ([paper](http://ieeexplore.ieee.org/xpl/articleDetails.jsp?arnumber=1143830)), for Direction-of-Arrival (DOA) estimation with microphone arrays. It is a port of [pyMUSIC](https://github.com/amjadsaadeh/pyMUSIC), the implementation written for empirical investigations of MUSIC in my master thesis. Pure Rust, no LAPACK. ## Features - Narrowband MUSIC: covariance → noise subspace (Hermitian eigendecomposition via `faer`) → pseudo-spectrum `1 / ‖Eₙᴴ a(θ)‖²` → peak picking. - Multi-source peak picking (circular local maxima, highest first). pyMUSIC's `getSourceAngles` clustered all estimates around the first peak; this is fixed here. - IFB-MUSIC (wideband): per-bin cross-spectral matrices from an STFT, narrowband spectra combined by geometric mean. - FFT-based analytic signal (Hilbert transform) and STFT helpers. ## Usage ```rust use musicrs::MusicEstimator; use nalgebra::DMatrix; // Default: Kinect 4-mic linear array, 720 angle steps over [0, 2π), 16 kHz let estimator = MusicEstimator::default(); // 4 × N real-valued microphone samples, e.g. read from a WAV file let data: DMatrix = /* ... */; // Narrowband DOA of one 1400 Hz source, in radians let angles = estimator.estimate_doa_from_real(&data, 1, 1400.0)?; // Wideband: IFB-MUSIC spectrum over chosen STFT bins (nfft = 160 → 100 Hz bins) let (spectrum, angles) = estimator.ifb_music_spectrum(&data, 160, 1, Some(&[14]))?; ``` Bad input (wrong channel count, NaN, silence, too many sources, an unusable angle grid, …) is returned as a `MusicError`. For other arrays use `MusicEstimator::new(antenna_positions, angle_steps_num, search_interval, sample_rate)` with `[x, y]` positions in metres. If you already have complex (analytic) data, call `estimate_doa` directly. ### Things to keep in mind - A linear array cannot distinguish θ from 360° − θ; restrict `search_interval` to [0, π] if you want a single answer. - IFB-MUSIC only sees frequencies up to Nyquist (`sample_rate / 2`); a tone recorded above Nyquist is aliased and its DOA cannot be recovered from the STFT bins. - Running IFB-MUSIC over *all* bins on a narrowband signal is dominated by noise-only bins; select the bins that carry signal energy. ## Performance vs pyMUSIC and numpy The same calls on the same recordings (1400 Hz, 40°), from the real-valued samples to the result, in three implementations: - **pyMUSIC**, run unmodified; - **numpy (vectorized)**, pyMUSIC's algorithm written the way numpy is meant to be used ([`bench/bench_numpy.py`](bench/bench_numpy.py)): the same analytic signal, `np.linalg.eig` and steering vectors, but in `float64`, with all 720 angles in one array operation, on one thread. Times the original [pyMUSIC](https://github.com/amjadsaadeh/pyMUSIC) and musicrs on the

`# Runtime benchmark: musicrs vs pyMUSIC and numpy

Times three implementations of the same algorithm on the same calls and recordings, keeps
every timed call, and summarises the distributions. The results and charts are in the
top-level README, section *Performance vs pyMUSIC and numpy*.

- **pyMUSIC**: the original [pyMUSIC](https://github.com/amjadsaadeh/pyMUSIC), unmodified
  (\`bench_pymusic.py\`).
- **numpy (vectorized)**: pyMUSIC's algorithm written idiomatically in numpy
  (\`bench_numpy.py\`). pyMUSIC spends almost all of its time in a Python loop that builds every
  steering vector element by element in \`float128\` with \`np.matrix\`, so on its own it
  measures how pyMUSIC is written, not what Python can do. This one keeps the same analytic
  signal, \`np.linalg.eig\`, eigenvector order, steering vectors and peak, but works in
  \`float64\` and builds the steering vectors of all angles in one array operation each call

# Runtime benchmark: musicrs vs pyMUSIC and numpy

Times three implementations of the same algorithm on the same calls and recordings, keeps
every timed call, and summarises the distributions. The results and charts are in the
top-level README, section *Performance vs pyMUSIC and numpy*.

- **pyMUSIC**: the original [pyMUSIC](https://github.com/amjadsaadeh/pyMUSIC), unmodified
  (`bench_pymusic.py`).
- **numpy (vectorized)**: pyMUSIC's algorithm written idiomatically in numpy
  (`bench_numpy.py`). pyMUSIC spends almost all of its time in a Python loop that builds every
  steering vector element by element in `float128` with `np.matrix`, so on its own it
  measures how pyMUSIC is written, not what Python can do. This one keeps the same analytic
  signal, `np.linalg.eig`, eigenvector order, steering vectors and peak, but works in
  `float64` and builds the steering vectors of all angles in one array operation each call
  (nothing is cached between calls). It runs on one BLAS thread, as musicrs runs on one
  thread. Before timing each case, it checks its result against pyMUSIC's on the same
  recording (spectrum within a relative 1e-6, same peak up to the θ / 2π − θ ambiguity of the
  linear array) and stops if they differ.
- **musicrs** (`examples/bench_pymusic.rs`).

## Workloads

All use the 1400 Hz / 40° recordings in `tests/data/single-source/` (4 channels, 16 kHz)
and the default estimator (Kinect array, 720 angles over [0, 2π)).

| Workload | pyMUSIC | numpy (`bench_numpy.py`) | musicrs | Recordings |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `narrowband` | `MUSICEst.getSourceAngles(data, 1, 1400)` | `source_angles(data, 1, 1400)` | `estimate_doa_from_real(&data, 1, 1400.0)` | 1 s, 2 s |
| `ifb_one_bin` | `IFBMUSICSpectrum(data, pos, 160, bins=[14])` | `ifb_music_spectrum(data, 160, [14])` | `ifb_music_spectrum(&data, 160, 1, Some(&[14]))` | 1 s, 2 s |
| `ifb_all_bins` | `IFBMUSICSpectrum(data, pos, 160, bins=range(1, 81))` | `ifb_music_spectrum(data, 160, range(1, 81))` | `ifb_music_spectrum(&data, 160, 1, Some(&(1..=80)))` | 1 s |

Each call includes everything from the real-valued samples to the result: analytic signal
or STFT, covariance, eigendecomposition and the spectrum. Reading the WAV file is not timed.
`ifb_all_bins` lists the 80 non-DC bins explicitly because pyMUSIC's `bins=None` would also
include DC and musicrs's would not. It runs on the 1 s recording only: one pyMUSIC call
takes about 11 s, and the cost is the 720-angle spectrum per bin, not the recording length.

All harnesses make 3 untimed warm-up calls, then time every call on its own
(`time.perf_counter_ns` / `std::time::Instant`) and write it to a CSV. pyMUSIC gets 200
samples per case (30 for `ifb_all_bins`), numpy and musicrs 1000. pyMUSIC runs unmodified with
`np.linalg.eig`; the only shim is the Python-2 index fix in pySoundToolbox, as in
`tests/golden/generate_golden.py`.

## Statistics

`analyze.py` reports mean ± stddev and the median for every case, and investigates the
shape of the distribution, because scheduling noise (preemption, interrupts, frequency
changes) only ever adds time and so appears as a right tail rather than as symmetric
spread:

- spread: MAD, p5/p95, min/max, coefficient of variation (stddev / mean);
- shape: skewness, excess kurtosis, Shapiro-Wilk tests on t and on log t, and whether a
  normal or a log-normal fit has the lower AIC;
- outliers: calls slower than median + 3 robust sigmas (1.4826 · MAD), their share, and the
  *tail excess*, how much they raise the mean over the mean of the other calls.

A small gap between mean and median and a small tail excess mean scheduling has little
influence on the result; the median is then a fair single number, and the mean ± stddev
an honest one.

## Reproduce

Run the three benchmarks one after the other on an otherwise idle machine, so they do not
compete for cores:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/amjadsaadeh/pyMUSIC /path/to/pyMUSIC
git clone https://github.com/Trion/pySoundToolbox /path/to/pySoundToolbox

cargo run --release --example bench_pymusic -- bench/results/musicrs.csv      # ~1 min
uv run --python 3.10 --with 'numpy==1.23.5' python -I bench/bench_pymusic.py \
    /path/to/pyMUSIC /path/to/pySoundToolbox bench/results/pymusic.csv        # ~10 min
uv run --python 3.10 --with 'numpy==1.23.5' python -I bench/bench_numpy.py \
    /path/to/pyMUSIC /path/to/pySoundToolbox bench/results/numpy.csv          # ~1 min
uv run --python 3.12 --with numpy --with scipy --with matplotlib \
    python -I bench/analyze.py
```

`BENCH_SCALE=0.1` scales every sample count down for a quick check (all harnesses).
`analyze.py` writes `bench/results/summary.{csv,md}` and the charts in `docs/`.
`bench/results/environment.txt` records the machine and the musicrs commit the committed
results come from; re-run all three after a change to musicrs, so the README never compares
one implementation's old numbers with another's new ones.

content.text:
I've made the benchmark compare musicrs against a vectorized numpy version of the same algorithm as well as pyMUSIC, re-run all three, and rewritten the README section. It's two commits on `fix/benchmark-fairness`, not pushed yet.

## Results

All three were run one after another on the current code:

| Workload | pyMUSIC | numpy (vectorized) | musicrs | musicrs vs numpy |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Narrowband · 1 s | 160 ms | 3.03 ms | 6.29 ms | 2.1× slower |
| Narrowband · 2 s | 158 ms | 5.02 ms | 13.4 ms | 2.7× slower |
| IFB, 1 bin · 1 s | 144 ms | 512 µs | 1.12 ms | 2.2× slower |
| IFB, 1 bin · 2 s | 149 ms | 855 µs | 2.48 ms | 2.9× slower |
| IFB, 80 bins · 1 s | 11.56 s | 18.8 ms | 5.43 ms | 3.5× faster |

The README no longer claims a Rust-over-Python speedup. It says musicrs is 12×–2,129× faster than pyMUSIC because of how pyMUSIC is written, 2–3× slower than idiomatic numpy on single-spectrum calls, and 3.5× faster when many bins are processed. The old musicrs results were measured before PRs #23 and #26, which is why its own numbers changed too: single-bin IFB got slower and 80-bin IFB about 3× faster.

## What's in the commits

1. **`bench/bench_pymusic.py`:** with `BENCH_SCALE` set, the second recording of each workload was scaled twice, so it got too few samples. Full runs were not affected.
2. **The numpy baseline and the rest:**
   - **`bench/bench_numpy.py`:** pyMUSIC's algorithm (same analytic signal, `np.linalg.eig`, steering vectors and peak) in `float64`, with all angles computed at once on one BLAS thread. Nothing is cached between calls. Before timing each case it checks its result against pyMUSIC's and stops if they differ; every case matched to a relative difference below 1e-7.
   - **`bench/analyze.py`:** handles three implementations. The table now has a "musicrs speedup" column relative to each of the others.
   - **Main chart:** now a dot plot on a log time axis, because on the old linear bar chart numpy and musicrs would be invisible next to 11.5 s. I checked both light and dark renders.
   - **Distribution chart:** now three columns.
   - **Docs:** the README section and `bench/README.md` are rewritten, and the distribution bullets updated from the new statistics. Run to run, the numbers vary by about ±20%, so I widened the README's stated uncertainty from ±10%.
   - **`environment.txt`:** now records the musicrs commit the results were measured on.
   - **`CLAUDE.md`:** the architecture line mentions the new harness.

I haven't done item 4, speeding up musicrs's narrowband path. The README now says plainly that musicrs is slower there, and says the Hilbert transform and covariance code are the likely cause, without having profiled them. I'd do that as a separate `fix/` branch, starting with a profile.

Should I push the branch and open a PR?
